1:
Whether the prophet's name is a name at all is asked first. Keil and Delitzsch report that his life is so unknown that it is disputed whether the word in the heading is a name or an ideal title given to the man who foretold the coming messenger; the ancient Greek read it as by the hand of his angel, and the Targumist glossed it with the name of a famous scribe of the return, a conjecture they trace to the spirit of the prophecy rather than evidence. Clarke reports the same conjecture and adds what can be dated: this is the last of the Jewish prophets, the temple begun under two predecessors standing complete in his day.

The word burden then divides them. Calvin says those who explain it as prophecy without exception are mistaken, since prophecy is not everywhere so called and the word always carries some judgment of God; the ungodly used the phrase as a proverb of reproach, meaning that the prophets brought nothing but threatenings, and so had their excuse for closing their ears. Gill takes the contrary view, that the book is so called not because it was heavy to carry or to bear, some of it being matter of joy, but because it was a message sent by the Lord and carried by his servant. Henry keeps both, dividing the term five ways: weight, repetition, reproach to those weary of it, ruin to the impenitent, and to those who welcome it a burden still, though light.

The opening claim of love is the ground of all that follows. Henry notes how abruptly the sermon begins, as though God meant, whatever reproofs were coming, to reconcile them to his love first. Gill enumerates the proofs: the choosing of them above all people, their continuance through a train of revolutions, their late deliverance.

The hatred of Esau makes the sharpest disagreement here. Gill calls it a negative rather than a positive hatred, yet carries it into the man's own case: God denied him special grace and left him to his lusts, so that he had no part in the inheritance above. Clarke denies exactly that: not a word is spoken here of the eternal state of either brother, what is spoken concerns their earthly possessions, and it concerns not the two brothers at all but the posterity of each. Ellicott takes the same side on other grounds: the nations and not the individuals are in view, and the ethical reason for either is not touched on, the hatred being mentioned merely for contrast.

When the mountains were laid waste, and by whom the rebuilding was thrown down, gets three answers. Ellicott infers from the older prophets that the subjugation was by the Babylonian king; Wesley dates it five years after the sacking of Jerusalem and adds that the one captivity returned and rebuilt its cities while the other never did. Clarke refers the throwing down to two later Jewish rulers who invaded that country, Henry to a far later attempt of the Jews themselves to rebuild their own city, thrown down by earthquakes and eruptions of fire. Ellicott quotes a modern writer who sets an ancient historian's description of the country as a bare desert against the cities named in a later age and the ruins reported by travellers, to show that Edom did build the desolate places and that they were thrown down.

Two smaller points close it. Ellicott prefers jackals to dragons for the creatures of the waste. On the last clause Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch agree against a common rendering: the phrase does not mean beyond the border but simply over or above it; Ellicott prefers the Lord is great to let him be magnified, and notes that the border of Israel is set on purpose against the border of wickedness.
6:
That the reproof falls on the priests, not the people, is dwelt on by two. Henry notes the reversal: these men, appointed to call others to account, are now called to account themselves, so that rulers in the house of God may know there is one above them; and he will not let the charge stay there, since what is said to the priests is said to all who profess a priesthood. Wesley puts it comparatively: undutifulness in the ignorant might have been excusable, whereas these men, whose business was to know God, despised him as the sons of Eli did and made others do the same.

The two relations at the head of the charge are expounded variously. Henry grounds the first in nature, a son honouring his father because he is his father, that law being written in the hearts of children before it was written on stone, while a servant's obligation is not natural but by compact and yet felt as duty. Gill keeps the plain rendering, that a son should honour by the laws of God and of man alike. Ellicott divides the fear in two: a servile fear, in which punishment and not fault is dreaded, and a filial fear, in which the fault is feared; what God requires is a reverence that loves to serve and a love that dreads to offend.

What the polluted bread was is a real dispute. Gill follows an ancient writer in taking it for the loaves of the presence and goes into the priestly labour of grinding, sifting, kneading and baking, the pollution lying in setting on the table what was not of fine flour or wanted frankincense. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott deny it outright on the same ground: the bread of the presence was never offered upon the altar. Ellicott adds the lexical case, that the word means food generally, carries the sense of flesh in a cognate tongue, and is used elsewhere of the fat of the peace offerings, so the phrase means food unfit to be offered. Wesley takes a middle course, either the meal offerings or everything presented to God.

The two then quarrel by name over the shape of the sentence. Keil and Delitzsch argue that the clause about offering cannot be the answer to the priests' question, since an answer could not be given in a participle, and read it as parallel to the address to the despisers of God's name, the answer coming at the words in that ye say. Ellicott quotes that construction and rejects it: the error lies in supposing that a participial phrase without the article can stand parallel to one defined by it, and the received version is perfectly correct. His own account is dramatic rather than grammatical, the priests catching the prophet up at his first clause, and he borrows a modern remark that the prophet puts their inward thought into hard words exhibiting the worm and the decay under the whited exterior.

On the blind and the lame they agree about the fault and differ about the motive. Clarke supposes they took the refuse beasts to ingratiate themselves with the people, bringing the sacrificial ordinances into contempt. Gill reports a Jewish reading in which the priests, given a blind lamb, said it was not evil but good enough to offer, because the table was contemptible. Ellicott would read when rather than if, notes that the practice was against the law, and explains the appeal that follows, whether such unsound animals could be offered to their own civil ruler with any hope of acceptance. On the title of that ruler both agree the word is foreign, Clarke identifying it as the term for a lieutenant or viceroy among three neighbouring empires and adding the melancholy note that neither then nor after was there a king in Israel.
9:
Whether the call to entreat God is meant seriously or in mockery is unsettled. Ellicott calls it severely ironical, and notes that the name for God is varied to set the divine judge against the human ruler just named: men who dare not treat their governor so can hope for no favour above. Gill offers both readings without choosing: a genuine exhortation to that part of their office which lay in interceding, they having been the means of the people's sin; or a taunt, that they should go and intercede and see how they succeed. Henry finds three senses in it: the ironical one, a real charge to stand in the gap for a land then eaten up with locusts, and a call to repentance, making up by fervency of prayer what was wanting in the worth of their sacrifices. Clarke takes it straight, an exhortation to pray while marks of displeasure lie on the land.

Ellicott presses two smaller renderings in the same verse. He would set the emphasis on the words by your means, and reads the question that follows not as whether God will regard the priests but whether he will, on their account, show favour to anyone at all, which is a practical denial that they can be worthy intercessors. Henry reaches the same charge plainly, that the rebukes of providence they were under were of their own procuring.

The verse about shutting the doors is read three ways. Gill reports the Jewish expositors, who take it as a wish that someone would shut the doors of the court against abominable offerings, and notes that the words for nothing do not stand where the received version puts them. Ellicott states the same construction, that the temple might as well be closed for all the pleasure the Lord takes in such offerings, and rejects it: the word even can only attach to the priests, which seems almost fatal to that rendering, so he keeps the received version, in which not one of them would do the smallest service unpaid. Henry takes the clause the other way, as evidence that God does not expect his servants to work for nothing, not a cup of cold water given for his honour losing its reward.

On the great name among the nations Ellicott argues from grammar to prophecy. The verse has no verb, so its participles may be rendered present or future; taken as present they meet the insurmountable difficulty that the name could in no sense be called great over all the earth in that age. He also refuses the suggestion that heathen rites are meant as offered ignorantly to the true God, nothing hinting at it and the sentiment being foreign to the older Scriptures. Gill reports the same suggestion from a Jewish writer and rejects it as flatly. Clarke states the conclusion without the argument: what is foretold is the abolition of the old sacrifices and a spiritual worship over the whole earth.

The one word for incense draws Ellicott into open controversy. He observes that the Hebrew is not used elsewhere in that sense and is more naturally rendered shall be burnt, so the promise is of an oblation burnt to the divine name, even a pure offering; and unless a universal material sacrifice is expected, both terms must be taken spiritually. Those who claim the verse for the use of incense in churches, he adds, must equally keep the yearly feast it is set beside in another prophet; and the word pure is emphatic not as marking a bloodless sacrifice but as the converse of polluted. Wesley takes the term as a legal word for a gospel duty covering prayers, praises and all gospel worship, and the pure offering as sincere against hypocrisy and holy against superstition. Keil and Delitzsch render the verses through without comment.
12:
The charge of profaning continues the contempt already described. Ellicott would put the verb in the present, that they profane the name, and reports the Jewish tradition that the pronoun stands as a euphemism to avoid saying me; he sets the conduct of these priests against the reverence just foretold of the heathen, the contempt showing in their not troubling to bring what the law prescribed. Clarke states the consequence baldly: having desecrated the worship they can hardly wonder at being cast off. Wesley spreads the blame, the people learning it by the priests' example, and notes that the saying is done by deportment rather than in words.

Whose weariness it was is not agreed. Gill gives two possibilities: the words may be the priests', complaining of a service for which they thought themselves poorly paid, the slaying, the clearing of ashes, the laying of wood and the kindling of fire; or the people's, who having carried a lamb on their shoulders said how weary they were with bringing it, hinting that the beast was so fat, which is the sense of the Jewish expositors and the Targum. Henry will not separate them, both being of that mind, the people grudging the charge of providing the sacrifice and the priests the pains of offering it; they thought the feasts came too thick and the purifying a penance, and it was their own hearts that made a weariness of what God had not. Wesley reduces it to the toil and drudgery of observing every point of the law.

The gesture that follows is caught two ways. Clarke reads a metaphor from cattle that dislike their fodder and blow strongly through the nose upon it, after which neither they nor any other beast will touch it. Ellicott renders it more simply that they puff at the service, treating with contempt what ought to have been their highest privilege.

One word in the list of bad offerings sets Ellicott a long investigation. The term rendered torn means elsewhere stolen, or robbed and so spoiled; he allows it may be a later word for torn, comparing an Arabic cognate, but observes that it is never so used in the later Jewish writings, while rabbinic tradition uses this very word when naming what is stolen as unfit for a burnt offering. He then conjectures a motive: a stolen animal would likely carry a mark making it impossible to sell without risking detection, so the thief makes a virtue of necessity and brings to the altar what he could not otherwise dispose of.

The curse at the close falls on the man who had something better and did not bring it. Wesley describes him as the hypocrite who would seem to offer of the best and puts God off with the worst, and glosses the male of the flock as the perfect animal required. Gill takes the word for a crafty and subtle man who contrives and speaks deceitfully, but records that some derive it from a root meaning to be able, so that the ancient Greek and Arabic versions read it of the man who is able to bring a proper offering and does not. Clarke widens it into a warning that such men can no more elude notice than escape the curse, citing as a complete comment the history of the couple who kept back part of the price; and he closes by observing that it was high time this corrupt service was broken up, God afterwards appearing to pay it no regard, for he sent them no other prophet. Henry meets the same point from the other side, that where the person is not accepted the offering will not be, so it is not enough to do what is good in the matter of it: it must be done from a right principle and for a right end.
